abstract: New York Fed Liberty Street Economics post (June 1, 2026) by Natalia Emanuel (NY Fed), Emma Harrington (UVA) and Amanda Pallais (Harvard), summarising their research on remote work and early-career outcomes. Their argument is a direct alternative to the AI explanation for weak young-graduate outcomes: remote work makes it harder for managers to train and mentor new hires, so firms on distributed teams hire fewer inexperienced workers. Using CPS data, they compare workers in 'remotable' occupations (e.g. software engineering) with those in non-remotable ones (e.g. mechanical engineering). The age gap in unemployment widened only in remotable occupations, where young graduates' unemployment rose almost 1 percentage point between 2017-19 and 2022-24; it began with the pandemic, before generative AI spread, and persists when occupations' AI exposure is held constant. A back-of-the-envelope calculation attributes 64 percent of the rise in unemployment for all young college graduates to remote work. Firm-level evidence from a Fortune 500 company shows less feedback and mentorship for workers separated from colleagues, and a hiring tilt toward experienced workers for distributed teams even after offices reopened. This is independent of, and consistent with, Lambert & Schindler (2026, SSRN), who also argue remote work confounds the AI-exposure pattern in junior hiring.
keyFindings: 64 percent: the share of the increase in unemployment for all young college graduates between 2017-19 and 2022-24 that remote work can explain, per the authors' back-of-the-envelope calculation.
Unemployment among those under 29 averaged 3.1 percent in 2017-19 and rose by 20 percent to 3.7 percent in 2022-25; for more experienced college graduates it dipped from 1.9 percent to 1.8 percent.
In remotable occupations, young people's unemployment rate increased by almost 1 percentage point between 2017-19 and 2022-24, while older workers' rate in remotable sectors marginally declined.
In non-remotable jobs, young graduates' relative unemployment ticked up in 2020 but returned to baseline soon afterward.
The rise in youth unemployment predates the rapid diffusion of AI, and the young-old gap persists in both remotable and non-remotable jobs when occupations' AI exposure is held constant.
Remote work has risen four-fold since the pandemic; the Fortune 500 firm studied hired more experienced workers for distributed-team positions even after offices reopened.
methodology: CPS microdata, college-educated workers, comparing ages 18-28 with 29+ across occupations classified as remotable or non-remotable with a standard teleworkability index; changes measured relative to 2019 and across 2017-19 vs 2022-24/25. The 64 percent figure is a back-of-the-envelope decomposition combining the remotable-occupation gap with young graduates' occupational concentration. Mechanism evidence comes from proprietary data on one Fortune 500 company (software engineers), including return-to-office mandates. US.
qualifiers: Tier 1: Federal Reserve Bank research blog by a Fed research economist and academic co-authors, summarising their own research. Caveats: the 64 percent is explicitly back-of-the-envelope, not a structural estimate. Remotability and AI exposure are strongly correlated across occupations (software is the canonical example of both), so separating them rests on the claim that the gap persists holding AI exposure constant; the post does not report the magnitude of that control. The mechanism evidence is one firm, software engineers at a Fortune 500 company, and may not generalise to other knowledge work. The authors say AI 'may play a more primary role' going forward. This does not refute exposure-based early-career estimates; it offers a competing explanation for the same pattern.
